extracted.intended_audience: readers of Horace; poets and writers looking for Horatian precepts on conduct, presentation, and subject-matter
extracted.subtask_description: Composing or studying Horace-style epistolary/lyric poetry and the attendant moral/social conduct: how and when to present work to patrons, preferred themes and dispositions (moderation, country life, virtue), and manners toward superiors and friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presenting poems to a patron with discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Present these volumes to Augustus sealed up if he shall be in health, if in spirits, finally, if he shall ask for them; do not offend out of zeal to me, and industriously bring an odium upon my books by being an agent of violent officiousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only present the poems at a proper opportunity and with due decorum; avoid excessive zeal or public display that would make the poet (or their works) a laughingstock. Keep the bundle discreetly carried (avoid clumsy or conspicuous handling), act when solicited or invited, and leave promptly after accomplishing the errand. Examples/imagery: 'lest you happen to carry my bundle of books under your arm, as a clown does a lamb... Solicited with much entreaty, do your best. Finally, get you gone... take care you do not stumble, and break my orders.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Value virtue above wealth, fame, and pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: If virtue alone can confer happiness, discarding pleasures, strenuously pursue it. To admire nothing is almost the one and only thing, Numicius, which can make and keep a man happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making external goods (silver, statues, applause, money, popularity) the chief aim; they are transient and subject to reversal. The wise man seeks virtue even if called fool or unjust by others. Examples: comparisons of riches, applause, and fame with the permanence of virtue; warnings about being stupefied by fear of losing external goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be indifferent to praise and blame (steady temper of mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be stung by false reproaches nor elated by honor conferred by the crowd; preserve an even temper and measure yourself by reason, not the popular voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace argues that public opinion can give or take honors; the wise should not depend on it. He uses examples: being called 'wise and good' today might be revoked tomorrow. The good man acts by justice and conscience rather than seeking public approbation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure yourself by your own proper foot and standard
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a truth, that every one ought to measure himself by his own proper foot and standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid imitating others' stations or ambitions; choose a life and pursuits suited to your temperament and resources. Example: Vulteius Maena's story—he became unhappy when he tried to live beyond his original disposition/condition and should have returned to his former life when losses exposed the mismatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the country life and simplicity to excessive urban ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: The country is more agreeable to nature and more friendly to liberty; trees, pure waters, and temperate air are preferable to the city's envious cares and excessive desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace praises rural retreat for temperate climate, simplicity, freedom from envy, and health. He advises choosing a plot suited to nature and warns that admiration of great things makes one unwilling to resign them. Repeated images across epistles: praise of Tibur, Tarentum, farm descriptions, and contrasts between country and city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in wealth accumulation—money should not lead life
rubrics_metrics.description: Accumulated money is the master or slave of each owner, and ought rather to follow than to lead the twisted rope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wealth pursued as an end makes its owner anxious and enslaved; one should avoid letting the desire to increase fortune supplant virtue and leisure. Anecdotes: Lucullus' cloaks, the scarce house where nothing superfluous exists, and the warning that if wealth alone made happiness one should seek to be first and last in amassing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate friendships with the great modestly and tactfully
rubrics_metrics.description: The friendship of great men is a laudable acquisition, yet their favors are ever to be solicited with modesty and caution. If poor, you must pay respects to the great; seek to be acceptable but avoid obsequiousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace contrasts two attitudes (Aristippus who courts the great for advantage vs. the cynic who scorns them) and favors a pragmatic modesty: play the buffoon or flatter when advantageous, but retain self-respect. Use tact in social climbing; being serviceable and agreeable can gain patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return to previous, more fitting pursuits when you recognize a mismatch
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as a man perceives how much the things he has discarded excel those which he pursues, let him return in time, and resume those which he relinquished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Vulteius Maena story as model: adopting a life unsuited to your nature leads to misery; restoration to a former, fitting life is honorable. For writers/poets: pursue the life/work that fits your character rather than chasing ill-fitting ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contentment derives from fitting one's disposition, bodily health, and simple comforts
rubrics_metrics.description: He that has the use of his belly, back, and feet is not poor; if it is well with your body and basic needs, regal wealth adds nothing greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace repeatedly emphasizes bodily health, simple fare, and temperate living as foundations of happiness. For a writer, attend to health and moderate comforts; do not sacrifice well-being for futile pursuits. Examples: debates on bathing places, hunting/sea comforts, and preference for plain bread over luxurious food.
